name: Auburn
headline: Auburn, where three highways meet
and the first liquid-fueled rocket flew.
answer: Auburn is a Worcester County town of 16,889 people (2020 Census), incorporated in 1778 as Ward and renamed Auburn in 1837. Its 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 78% of homes as single-family detached. The Massachusetts Turnpike, I-290 and I-395 meet in town, WRTA buses run to Worcester, and the nearest MBTA station is Worcester Union Station on the Framingham/Worcester Line.
meta: Auburn, MA: 1778 town where I-90, I-290 and I-395 meet, with mill villages, Goddard's 1926 rocket site, 2025 Warren Group prices and FY2026 tax rates.
overview: Auburn was incorporated on April 10, 1778, from parts of Worcester, Sutton, Leicester and Oxford, and named Ward for General Artemas Ward; most of it had been Worcester's South Parish, first settled in 1714. In 1837 the Post Office complained that Ward was too similar to the nearby town of Ware, and the town became Auburn. Wellington, Dark and Kettle Brooks run north and east through town toward the Blackstone River, and in the 19th century they powered mill villages: Jeremy Stone built a brick woolen mill and worker housing at Stoneville in 1834, and Pondville's mills made yarn and satinets. The Norwich and Worcester Railroad began service through Auburn in 1840, and by 1900 a streetcar line ran from Worcester along Southbridge and Central Streets toward Oxford.

On March 16, 1926, Robert H. Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket from his aunt's farm on Pakachoag Hill. The site is now inside the town-owned Pakachoag Golf Course on Upland Street, where a granite marker beside the ninth fairway shows the spot; it was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1966. The town's commercial center is Drury Square, where Auburn and Southbridge Streets meet: one- to three-story buildings set back behind parking, with Auburn High School on the northwest side of Southbridge Street and the public library, Goddard Park and fire headquarters on the southeast side. The Auburn Mall, opened in 1971 at 385 Southbridge Street, sits on Route 12 near the junction of the Turnpike, I-290 and I-395.

Auburn's 2024 Housing Production Plan, prepared with the Central Massachusetts Regional Planning Commission and approved by the state for July 2024 to July 2029, counts 6,979 year-round housing units. Two former elementary schools, the Mary D. Stone and Julia Bancroft schools, have been redeveloped as rental apartments under comprehensive permits: 55 mixed-income units at Mary D. Stone, opened in May 2022, and 60 units at Julia Bancroft. The plan reports 366 units, or 5.24%, on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory in 2023, and sets a goal of about 35 qualifying units a year. It also lists a strategy to comply with the state's MBTA Communities zoning law, and the state's compliance list (as of October 21, 2026) includes Auburn.

housing.text: Auburn's 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 78% of homes as single-family detached, 3% in two-family buildings, 7% in buildings of 3 to 9 units and 4% in buildings of 10 or more (2021 American Community Survey). At the 2020 Census, 82% of occupied homes were owner-occupied and 18% rented, and about 22% of the stock was built before 1940.

villages.name: Auburn Center
villages.line: The civic center on Central Street, where the First Congregational church and first town hall replaced the burned meetinghouse in 1896 and the Merriam Library was built in 1910; bungalows and 1930s and 1940s Colonial Revival houses cluster nearby.

villages.name: Drury Square
villages.line: The commercial district where Auburn and Southbridge Streets meet, with low-rise shopping, Goddard Park, the library and fire headquarters, and the Auburn Mall within its study area.

villages.name: Stoneville
villages.line: A mill village in the north of town, built around Jeremy Stone's 1834 brick woolen mill, with two-story double-chimney worker houses, one-story duplexes from about 1860, St. Joseph's Church (1869) and a few triple-deckers.

villages.name: Pondville
villages.line: A mill village in the east of town where a saw and grist mill turned to yarn in the 1850s and later made satinets and cassimeres.

villages.name: West Auburn
villages.line: A village around the Warren tannery, founded in 1777, with an 1825 schoolhouse at Central and Prospect Streets.

villages.name: Pakachoag
villages.line: The hill area at the Worcester line, site of a 17th-century Christian Indian village and later of Goddard's 1926 launch, with 1880s and 1890s side-passage houses and 20th-century bungalows.

commute.text: Auburn has no commuter rail station of its own; the nearest is Worcester Union Station, the western end of the Framingham/Worcester Line. I-290 begins in Auburn as the continuation of I-395, at a junction with the Turnpike, Route 12 and Route 20. WRTA Routes 27, 29 and 42 run from Worcester's Central Hub to Auburn Street, the Auburn Mall, Southbridge Street and Washington Street.

places.name: Goddard Rocket Launching Site
places.line: The spot where Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926, marked by granite beside the ninth fairway of the town-owned Pakachoag Golf Course on Upland Street; a National Historic Landmark since 1966.

places.name: Goddard Memorial Park
places.line: A park beside the fire department headquarters in Drury Square with a model of Goddard's rocket and a Polaris A-1 missile.

places.name: Auburn Historical Museum
places.line: The 1922 Tuttle Square School at 41 South Street, a Craftsman bungalow-style building leased to the Auburn Historical Society in 1999 and listed on the National Register in 2002; exhibits cover Robert Goddard, Nipmuc artifacts and the town's schools and farms.

places.name: Eddy Pond
places.line: A 100-acre great pond and impoundment of Dark Brook, with a town-managed concrete boat ramp off South Street; fish include largemouth bass, chain pickerel and yellow perch.

places.name: Joseph Stone House
places.line: A First Period, one-and-a-half-story timber-frame house at 35 Stone Street, begun in 1729 with two bays added in 1790; listed on the National Register in 1986.

places.name: Auburn Mall
places.line: A single-level mall of 583,739 square feet at 385 Southbridge Street, opened in 1971 and owned by Simon Property Group, with Macy's and a Reliant Medical Group center as anchors.

history.text: Parts of Worcester, Sutton, Leicester and Oxford were incorporated on April 10 as the Town of Ward, named for General Artemas Ward.
Jeremy Stone built a brick woolen mill and worker housing at Stoneville; it became the Stoneville Manufacturing Company's cotton mill in 1839.
The town was renamed Auburn after the Post Office complained that Ward was too similar to the nearby town of Ware.
Robert H. Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket from Pakachoag Hill on March 16.
The Goddard Rocket Launching Site was designated a National Historic Landmark on November 13.

The town's Historical Tax Rates page (https://www.auburnma.gov/835/Historical-Tax-Rates) gives 2025 as $14.29 residential and $16.10 commercial. No residential exemption is mentioned.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Auburn, MA?
faq.a: The median single-family sale price in Auburn for calendar year 2025 was $475,000, across 188 sales, up from $429,000 across 189 sales in 2024, according to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report. The condo median was $345,000 across 19 sales.

No. Auburn has no MBTA station of its own; the nearest is Worcester Union Station, the western end of the Framingham/Worcester Line. WRTA Routes 27, 29 and 42 connect Auburn with Worcester's Central Hub.
Auburn Public Schools, which serves prekindergarten through grade 12. Review its profile with DESE, and confirm school assignment for any address with the district.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Auburn?
faq.a: For fiscal year 2026 the town lists a residential rate of $14.24 per $1,000 of assessed value and a commercial rate of $15.83, according to the Auburn Assessing Division.
The Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90), I-290 and I-395 meet in Auburn, where I-290 begins as the continuation of I-395. Route 12 (Southbridge Street) and US Route 20 also cross the town.

faq.q: Where did Robert Goddard launch his rocket?
faq.a: On Pakachoag Hill in Auburn, on March 16, 1926. The launch site is inside the town-owned Pakachoag Golf Course on Upland Street, marked beside the ninth fairway, and has been a National Historic Landmark since 1966.

notes: Written 2026-10-22. Sources: Wikipedia (town article, Goddard Rocket Launching Site, Tuttle Square School, Joseph Stone House, Auburn Mall (Massachusetts), Interstate 290), the 1984 MHC reconnaissance report (OCR-scanned and about 40 years old; used for village history and housing types only), the 2024 Housing Production Plan on mass.gov, the town's Robert Goddard, Assessing Division and Historical Tax Rates pages, the 2016 Massachusetts Downtown Initiative report on Drury Square, the MassWildlife Eddy Pond page, the WRTA community profiles PDF (https://therta.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/WRTA_CommunityProfiles_all.pdf, undated; routes 27, 29 and 42), the MBTA Worcester stop page, DESE (district code 00170000, PK-12), and the state's MBTA Communities compliance list (https://www.mass.gov/doc/mbta-communities-district-compliance-letters/download, 'As of October 21, 2026', no. 10 Auburn). Interstate junction facts are from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_290_(Massachusetts). Market: both single-family and condo rows read directly from the Warren Group PDF in two fetches; the condo row also matches tools/data/condo-2025.json. Tax: the Assessing Division heading reads '2026 TAX RATES' without saying 'fiscal'; FY2026 is inferred, since the historical page's 2025 rates ($14.29/$16.10) match the prior year. Fair-housing judgment calls: the Mary D. Stone and Julia Bancroft redevelopments are described in the HPP as mixed-income senior rental housing; the age restriction is left out (as in the Westborough record) and they are described only as rental apartments. The Council on Aging van service in the WRTA profile is left out because eligibility is age-based. Left out or unconfirmed: the HPP's figure of 'about 52% built before 1960' was a derived calculation, not a stated figure, so only the 22% pre-1940 share is used; the HPP's Eastland Partners 40B project (324 apartments expected by early 2025) was left out because its location and completion could not be confirmed; the 2021 Open Space and Recreation Plan PDF would not load, so ponds other than Eddy Pond, the Pakachoag Hiking Trail and the Pappas Recreation Complex have no details; the Historical Museum page lists its address as '41 S Street', and the Tuttle Square School article gives 41 South Street. The Merriam Library (1910, MHC) and the 'Auburn Free Public Library' in the Drury Square report may be the same institution; this was not confirmed, so the record does not equate them. Goddard Memorial Park's model and Polaris missile come from the town's Wikipedia article only. The town's MBTA Communities category and district acreage were not found.
